analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in finance and insurance at 36.5% in the latest reading, down from 40.0% in the prior period. The survey asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks, and the sector covered is NAICS 52, which spans banking, insurance, and related financial activities. The decline between periods is worth noting, but the survey does not explain why the share fell.

What banks actually deploy AI for is older than the current generative wave. Fraud detection and credit models have been in production for decades, and per the Federal Reserve, credit and anti-money laundering models have operated under SR 11-7 model risk management guidance since 2011. That means banking is the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade. The newer frontier, per this site's coverage, is generative AI in customer service and compliance work, layered on top of those established model risk controls.

The Evident AI Banking Index is the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard. It scores the major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics, including talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. The index treats AI capability as something measurable across an institution rather than a single tool purchase, which reflects how banks think about the technology as an organizational capability.

On the open model side, The World of AI tracks the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, download counts, and release dates refreshed daily. These are models tuned for financial text, and the catalogue gives a view of what is publicly available rather than what sits inside bank firewalls. The page notes the tag provenance is stated, meaning the financial tuning labels come from the model cards themselves.

The regulatory posture is already established rather than emerging. Treasury has produced a report on AI in financial services covering uses, opportunities, and risks, and that report frames the US supervisory conversation. The Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 guidance from 2011 remains the operative model risk framework for credit and AML models, so banks adding generative AI to service and compliance functions are doing so inside a supervisory structure that has existed for well over a decade.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a sector where adoption is measurable but not uniform, where the governance burden is real and pre-existing, and where public benchmarks and open model catalogues exist for orientation. The sources here do not report ROI figures or vendor concentration, so those questions remain open on this evidence.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The World of AI reports that this page catalogues the 1,000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub. Each entry includes its licence, download count, and release date, and the list is refreshed daily. The data comes from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, and every model links to its own Hub page. The page was last verified on 22 September 2026.
